source.title: How Does DPO Reduce Toxicity? A Mechanistic Neuron-Level Analysis
source.authors: Yu-Shi Yang; Filip Sondej; Harry Mayne; Andrew Lee; Adam Mahdi

page_placements.theme: Function is distributed: units chosen by correlation, selectivity or a well-scoring explanation are often causally insufficient, and populations or subspaces carry the concept

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron-level explanations and reports results about how DPO changes toxicity, but it does not test the listed versions concerning neuron job shares, polysemantic neurons, attribution graphs, or explanation scoring.
record.gate_note: The study reports neuron-level toxicity measurements and activation-patching outcomes, recorded below as findings about the claim's subject that none of its listed versions specifically covers. It does not audit whether neuron poles have one or more identifiable jobs, test explanations on held-out activations, build attribution graphs, or score explanations on new text. Probe validation accuracies and hyperparameter-selection results are not included because they do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study asks how DPO lowers toxicity, using a linear probe, per-neuron projections and activation patching in four LLMs. It does not estimate shares of neurons with one or more jobs, analyse vision neurons, build attribution graphs, or score neuron explanations against held-out activations. Its only link to the claim is a one-line discussion remark that the toxic-neuron explanation relies on a monosemantic view of neurons, citing Elhage et al. 2022. That makes it a discussion, not a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors find that toxic neurons account for only 2.5%–24% of DPO's toxicity reduction, and that DPO instead spreads small activation shifts across all MLP neurons. They identify four neuron groups whose combined patching matches or exceeds DPO, and propose a probe-based activation-editing method that beats DPO without weight updates. They also argue that the earlier explanation rests on a disputed monosemantic view of neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies DPO toxicity mechanisms using linear toxicity probes, neuron contribution measurements, and activation patching; it does not use the original neuron-pole audit or explanation-testing recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported patch effects vary by model and by neuron selection: token-identified toxic neurons and top-256 toxic-aligned vectors account for different shares of DPO's toxicity reduction.

fits_no_version.finding: In GPT-2-Medium, 74.7% of the 128 top toxic-aligned value vectors have conflicting alignment signs across three SVD toxicity directions. 74.3% of neurons show inconsistent projection changes after DPO across those directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single value vectors align with different, opposing aspects of a concept subspace, so a neuron's label depends on which concept direction is used.

fits_no_version.finding: Toxic-labelled neurons explain only a small share of DPO's toxicity reduction (0.41%–23.9%). The effect is spread across roughly half of all MLP neurons (52–58% reduce their toxicity projection).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A behavioural change from fine-tuning is carried by small shifts spread over many neurons, not by a few neurons whose job is that concept.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2024
record.problems: The analysis uses a single linear toxicity probe and assumes neuron contributions can be estimated by projection; the authors note that toxicity may occupy multiple directions and report conflicting alignments under their initial subspace analysis. Patching uses mean activations from the study's prompt set. No uncertainty intervals are reported for the main patching results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Table 19 perplexity and F1 results, DPO and steering baselines, and activation-editing results were left out because they measure language quality or the performance of the study's own editing method rather than the listed neuron-interpretability claim. Appendix figures and further activation-shift analyses were also omitted because they do not test a listed version.

untested.parts: No audit of job shares for neuron poles, and Qwen3-32B is not studied.
No job-share audit in any model. The four dense models (355M–8B) are used only for toxicity mechanisms; no MoE or trillion-scale models.
No InceptionV1, cat-and-car neuron, pose or recursive-generalization analysis.
No estimate of the interpretable-neuron share as tools or architectures vary. The remark that smooth activations let many weak neurons contribute to toxicity is not a test of interpretability shares.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with a replacement model.
Toxic neurons are labelled from logit-lens top tokens, but the study never checks whether those labels predict where the neurons fire.

missing.what: Share of neurons whose sign-flipped value vectors align with conflicting SVD toxicity directions (74.7%), and share with inconsistent projection change after DPO (74.3%).
missing.versions: none (closest to the claim's subject; does not test a version)

missing.what: Share of MLP neurons that reduce versus increase their toxicity projection after DPO.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are correctly linked to none; no verdicts are given. The study's neuron 'interpretability' rests only on logit-lens tokens of value vectors, judged by GPT-4o. The Table 2 and Table 19 DPO figures for Mistral disagree (0.191 vs 0.221).

versions.untested_parts: No estimate of the shares of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or unresolved jobs.
No cross-model or scale audit of neuron job shares, including no MoE or trillion-parameter models.
No analysis of InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
No vision-model interpretability estimates or comparison of architecture, regularization, and tools as causes of interpretability.
No attribution graphs or comparison with a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
No test of whether explanations derived from activating examples predict where neurons fire.
No automated neuron-explanation scoring by simulating activations on new text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It discusses neuron-level localisation of toxicity in a different setting and does not test the claim.

tranche.reason: The study analyses how DPO reduces toxicity (probe, per-neuron projections, activation patching). It does not measure neuron interpretability shares, vision neurons, attribution graphs or explanation scoring, so it tests none of V1-V7.

source_check.notes: Rows match Table 3 (columns GPT-2, Llama, Gemma, Mistral). The paper calls both patch sets 'toxic neurons': the toxic-token sets give 0.41%-19.7% and the top-256 sets 2.47%-23.9%. The paper's headline '2.5% to 24%' fits only the top-256 row. 52%-58% is the rounded Table 18 range (51.75% Gemma to 58.49% GPT-2). All rows sit under versions none.
